transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?
I get stuck in front of the mirror or looking at photos of myself, trying to fix how I look. It's starting to mess with my work and my runs.

When you get stuck checking or trying to fix your appearance, does it feel driven by repetitive unwanted thoughts that you can’t control, and do you do certain rituals to relieve the anxiety? Or is it more that you’ve been feeling generally down, with low interest or pleasure in things most days?

It’s definitely driven by these unstoppable thoughts about how crooked and battered my face looks, rather than just feeling down. I get completely stuck for hours zooming in on photos, staring in the mirror to shave and re-shave, and constantly asking my sister and kids if I look lopsided. It feels like a loop of trying to fix it that I just can't break out of.

Are these unwanted thoughts and rituals almost entirely about your appearance, or do you also have other obsessions or compulsive behaviors not related to how you look, like checking, counting, cleaning, or arranging things?

No, it's completely about how I look. I don't have any other habits like checking locks, counting, or cleaning. Everything I do, from the mirror-checking to shaving and picking at my skin, is just me trying to fix my crooked face.
Do you ever think your face really is deformed or obviously abnormal to other people, or is part of you aware that this fear might be exaggerated? How convinced are you, from 0 to 100%?

I'm not really sure how to put a percentage on it, but it feels incredibly real and convincing to me in the moment. When I'm looking in the mirror, I'm absolutely sure I look deformed, even if I sometimes wonder why other people don't seem to see it the same way.

opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance focused on the face, accompanied by repetitive behaviors aimed at checking, fixing, and seeking reassurance. These symptoms are appearance-focused rather than due to broader OCD symptoms or a primary depressive syndrome, and they are causing functional impairment at work and in running. This presentation is most consistent with body dysmorphic disorder (ICD-10 F45.2).
